summary: This informational document defines a set of algorithms that can be used with the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) protocol described in RFC 9052. Together with RFC 9052 it obsoletes RFC 8152.

eli5.summary: COSE is a lock-and-stamp system, and it needs actual locks to use. This document lists a starter set of locks and stamps that can be plugged into that system.

subtitle: The starter menu of signature, MAC, encryption and key-distribution algorithms for COSE messages.

tldr.problem: The COSE message structures need concrete algorithms to plug into them, with identifiers that fit in compact CBOR messages for constrained devices.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9053 assigns identifiers and usage rules for ECDSA and EdDSA signatures, HMAC and AES-CBC-MAC, AES-GCM, AES-CCM and ChaCha20/Poly1305 encryption, HKDF, key wrap, ECDH key agreement, and the key object parameters they use.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that, together with RFC 9052, obsoletes RFC 8152, and it has since been updated by RFC 9864.

today: RFC 9053 is an Informational document that, together with RFC 9052, obsoletes RFC 8152. It has been updated by RFC 9864.

sections.title: Role in the COSE Specification
sections.content:
CBOR is a data format designed to be small in both message size and implementation size, and it is used by several IETF working groups dealing with the Internet of Things. COSE adds message security on top of it. The core COSE specification has two documents: RFC 9052 holds the serialization structures and general procedures, and this document supplies an initial set of algorithms for those structures.

RFC 9053 was created by splitting RFC 8152. The sections on specific algorithms were moved here, the structure and processing rules went to RFC 9052, text was clarified, and the details of countersignatures were moved to a separate document. Together, the two new RFCs obsolete RFC 8152.

Each algorithm table lists a name, the value used on the wire (for example in the algorithm header parameter) and a short description. A GitHub project of test examples is also cited.
sections.eli5: One document describes the shape of the envelope. This one lists the kinds of locks and stamps you can put on it, each with a short number.

sections.title: Signature and MAC Algorithms
sections.content:
Two signature algorithms are defined. ECDSA comes as ES256 (-7), ES384 (-35) and ES512 (-36), working only with curves P-256, P-384 and P-521 encoded as EC2 keys. Implementations SHOULD use a deterministic version of ECDSA, which avoids reliance on a random number generator for the per-message value k. The RFC suggests pairing SHA-256 with P-256, SHA-384 with P-384 and SHA-512 with P-521. EdDSA is a single identifier (-8) usable with several curves, and only the pure EdDSA variant is used, not HashEdDSA.

For message authentication, HMAC is defined as HMAC 256/64 (4), HMAC 256/256 (5), HMAC 384/384 (6) and HMAC 512/512 (7). The first is truncated to a 64-bit tag for constrained environments. AES-CBC-MAC comes in four variants (14, 15, 25 and 26) with 128-bit or 256-bit keys and 64-bit or 128-bit tags, always with an all-zero IV.

For every algorithm, the RFC lists the checks to make on a COSE key: the kty field MUST be present and correct, an alg field if present MUST match, and key_ops if present MUST permit the operation, such as sign, verify, MAC create or MAC verify.
sections.eli5: A signature proves who wrote a message. A MAC proves nobody changed it. This part lists which signing pens and which tamper seals you may use, and gives each a number.

sections.title: Content Encryption Algorithms
sections.content:
Three content encryption families are defined, all AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data). AES-GCM has three identifiers, A128GCM (1), A192GCM (2) and A256GCM (3), with the nonce fixed at 96 bits and the tag fixed at 128 bits.

AES-CCM is the mode usually used in constrained environments. The RFC defines a matrix of eight algorithms (values 10 to 13 and 30 to 33) over two choices. L is the length field size, 16 bits (13-byte nonce, messages up to 216 bytes) or 64 bits (7-byte nonce). M is the tag size, 64 or 128 bits. The RFC counts in bits, noting that CCM itself counts in bytes, which causes confusion.

ChaCha20/Poly1305 (24) takes a 256-bit key and a 96-bit nonce. The RFC notes it is not AES and so would not suffer from future AES weaknesses, and that it is designed to be fast in software-only implementations.

Each has MUST-level limits. The key and nonce pair MUST be unique for every message. For AES-GCM the total number of messages for one key MUST NOT exceed 232. For AES-CCM the total number of block cipher operations MUST NOT exceed 261. The RFC also advises tracking failed decryptions.
sections.eli5: Encryption scrambles a message so only the right person can read it, and these algorithms also notice if someone tampered with it. The rule for all of them: never reuse the same key and nonce for two messages, like never using the same one-time code twice.

sections.title: Key Derivation and Key Distribution
sections.content:
A KDF turns a shared secret into usable keys. The RFC defines one, HKDF, in four flavours: HMAC with SHA-256, HMAC with SHA-512, and AES-MAC with 128-bit or 256-bit keys as the pseudorandom function. A COSE_KDF_Context structure binds the derived key to its context: the algorithm ID, information about the two parties (PartyU is the message creator, PartyV the receiver, unless the application says otherwise), public information including the key length in bits, and optional private information. Defining the parties this way yields different keys for each direction.

Content keys can then be delivered in several ways:

  • Direct (-6): the identified key is the content key; the key type MUST be Symmetric.
  • Direct with KDF (-10 to -13): a shared secret is run through HKDF. Either a salt or a PartyU nonce MUST be present.
  • AES Key Wrap (A128KW -3, A192KW -4, A256KW -5): the content key is wrapped by another key.
  • Direct ECDH (-25 to -28): Ephemeral-Static or Static-Static key agreement, always followed by HKDF.
  • ECDH with key wrap (-29 to -34): key agreement produces a key used to wrap the content key.

COSE has no Ephemeral-Ephemeral mode because COSE is not an online protocol and cannot set up ephemeral secrets on both sides. When ephemeral keys are used, the sender MUST generate a new one for every key agreement.
sections.eli5: Instead of mailing the actual key, two people can each combine a secret of their own to cook up the same key. Or one person can lock the message key in a small safe and send the safe.

sections.title: Key Objects and Capabilities
sections.content:
The COSE key object needs members defined for each key type. Four kty values are defined here: OKP (1, Octet Key Pair), EC2 (2, elliptic curve with x and y coordinates), Symmetric (4) and Reserved (0).

EC2 keys use crv, x, y and d. The y member may be a sign bit (CBOR false or true) to allow point compression, which can shrink a message for constrained use. OKP keys use crv, x and d. Symmetric keys use a single member k, and since they are meant to be transmitted, care is needed so they are never sent accidentally or insecurely. Applications MUST check that the curve and the key type are consistent.

The RFC also defines capabilities, an array describing what an algorithm or key type can do, similar to S/MIME capabilities. They can be used to advertise what a device supports or to confirm both sides use the same parameters.

Finally, the CBOR encoding for COSE_KDF_Context must use definite lengths and the shortest possible argument encoding. Applications MUST NOT generate or process a map that uses the same label twice.
sections.eli5: A key is stored in a small labelled card. The card says what kind of key it is, which curve it uses and holds the key bits. Another card type lists what a device is able to do.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Most security notes sit next to each algorithm. The overall section stresses protecting private key material. Using the same key for two different algorithms can leak information about the key, so keys should be restricted to a single algorithm, and the algorithm in a key structure should be strictly matched to the one in the message.

Using direct as a recipient algorithm together with a second recipient exposes the direct key to that second recipient, and RFC 9052 forbids combining direct recipients with other modes. With Static-Static ECDH or direct plus KDF and two recipients, the second recipient could forge a message that the first would wrongly treat as proof of origin. Adding a key wrap step avoids this.

Per-algorithm notes include the substitution attacks on ECDSA (changing the curve or hash used to verify), the replay-style risk of reusing an AES-GCM or AES-CCM nonce, and the weak points of CBC-MAC, which the fixed zero IV and length-aware encoding address. Public values differ between EdDSA and ECDH, so a key from one should not be used with the other.
sections.eli5: Never use one key for two different jobs, never reuse a one-time code, and be careful who else gets a copy of the shared key.
